title: Is This The End of The Friendly Trend?
summary:
Is This The End of The Friendly Trend? 

             
             
            Bonds weathered their biggest day of selling since September today and their only notable day of selling since the recent downtrend in rates began in mid-October. The blame game was simple: CPI was much higher than expected and there were no silver linings in the report's internal components. Multiple Fed speakers (including Warsh 2 weeks ago) have reiterated the Fed's focus on inflation as opposed to the labor market. Even before the data, Waller said a 0.3 core CPI reading could mean a 50bp rate hike in December (and 0.3 is what we got). Fed Funds Futures and shorter-dated Treasuries logically led the selling, but it was big enough to still hit 10yr yields for 10bps. The potential for Tuesday to mark a shift in the trend should be respected as a possibility, but not necessarily a foregone conclusion. We may have some extra volatility associated with the mid-week holiday closure and the true fate of the trend will depend on more than just inflation. That said, it definitely makes it less likely that the rally can continue without new fuel.

title: Mortgage Rate Sharply Higher After Inflation Data
summary: Rates enjoyed a remarkably calm winning streak over the past month with the worst single day resulting in a 0.06% increase for a top tier 30yr fixed loan and the average day seeing a 0.02% decline. That streak was dealt its first serious blow today following a hotter than expected in the Consumer Price Index (CPI)--a key inflation report.  Even though the Fed's official inflation target is based on Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE), we'll be waiting another 2 weeks for that report to come out for the month of October. CPI (the one we got today) always comes out earlier in the month and because much of the data flows through to the more robust PCE data set, CPI reliably produces more volatility for the bond/rate market.  Today's report showed broad-based price pressures with only a small handful of categories seeing any improvements. Naturally, the categories most closely tied to higher fuel prices were the worst, but many non-fuel-related categories were surprisingly high.  Given that the Fed explicitly said it was more focused on the inflation component of its job description at the moment (as opposed to the "full employment" component), we were expecting today's data to carry far more weight than last week's jobs report. The reaction was logical an immediate. When the dust settled, the average top tier 30yr fixed rate was 0.12% higher day over day at 7.30%.  While that's the largest one day increase in over a month, it's still quite a bit lower than the 7.6%+ levels seen in early October.   [thirtyyearmortgagerates]

title: No "Yeah Buts" in Today's CPI. It's All Bad For Bonds
summary:
Some inflation reports have counterpoints even if they appear high at first glance. This one is just all-around not great for bonds. It would be a genuine surprise to see a meaningful reversal from this morning's weakness without a major, unexpected news headline or massive stock sell-off. 
 Really the only way someone could try to find a silver lining would be to say that month-over-month inflation moved a hair lower in a few key categories, but considering last month's report saw very high readings in those categories, that silver might actually be a lightning bolt. As a reminder, there is no y/y CPI number today because of last year's gov shutdown. The asterisk below denotes an interpolated baseline from Sept/Nov 2025.   
 
 m/m Core CPI : .296 vs 0.22 f'cast 
 y/y Core CPI*: 2.8 vs 2.7 f'cast, 2.6 prev 
 Supercore: :   .399% 
 
 The bond market hit was immediate. As expected, shorter-term yields are hit hardest as they're the most closely related to Fed Funds Rate expectations. December's expected rate shot sharply higher in 2 phases.  The first came before the data when Fed's Waller (not Warsh) said they Fed should consider a 50bp hike if core CPI came it at 0.3% or higher. The second phase was in response to CPI itself. Markets are now pricing in a bit more than one full rate hike in December.
